doc.title: Keith Ingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

chapter: Working with American visitors and moving to the U.S.
title: Hearing Louis Armstrong and the jazz masters as entertainers
summary: Ingham recalls the thrill of Armstrong's All Stars, and says Ellington, Waller and Armstrong were entertainers, which bebop lacked.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: and suddenly you hear this trumpet playing Louis’ signature tune, behind the curtain [scats] “Sleepy Time Down South.” And you suddenly realize here is this guy, coming out, and the curtains parted and there he is. But the magic of hearing that trumpet behind the curtains, before. The sound came before the guy. And you see Louis of course. Just incredible. It’s magical. And I think those kind of guys had that love of entertaining as well, which I think bebop somehow didn’t have. I wouldn’t say they were playing down to an audience, but it was not that kind of music. Of course it has warmth, bop has a lot of beauty in it and that. But it doesn’t have that kind of charismatic thing that goes to an audience to entertain. And I think the great early jazz musicians, like Ellington, entertainer. Have you ever seen those shorts of Duke Ellington with the band? He’s playing the piano, looking at the camera, the hands are going like this, it was a great show. You’ve seen that drum kit Sonny Greer had out there?

The timps, the chimes, what a show — wonderful. And can you imagine Fats Waller, the piano player, you know you’ve seen him in movies, I mean as soon as he comes on he steals the whole scene, because you can’t take your eyes off him. You know he’s magnetic people. And I think they had that thing, you know, that quality of, you have an audience, you’ve got to go and entertain this audience, whether you’re playing jazz or anything. And a lot of those guys didn’t think of themselves as jazz players, they were just musicians. I think Bechet was like that.
That’s what Louis Armstrong said. He said he was an entertainer.

An entertainer, yeah. I think in all humility, it’s a really different thing. I think it’s the people who’ve come afterwards have made them these jazz Gods, but Louis, as you say, was an entertainer. He loved his public. Kept going. Like Basie. He kept going right through the end. Duke, the same thing. They had to get that audience.
